speaker: Noam Brown
title: Really Big Test-Time Compute in AI with OpenAI's Noam Brown
question: In frontier AI labs, why does nobody actually know the true capability ceiling of newly released models?
guest: We're going to pretty soon be at the point where you can tell a model to go work on a complex project for a month and come back with a state-of-the-art result. The problem is, if you want to evaluate what a model can do after running for a month, the only way to be fully sure is to actually run it for a month. If you want to know after six months, the only way to know fully is to run it for six months. Meanwhile, we're releasing new models every two or three months at this point. A model comes out, it takes two or three months to push it to its limits, and then another model comes out. So nobody actually knows what the ceiling of capabilities is for these models because nobody has run them long enough to really tell. The implications are pretty interesting: the only way for labs to fully evaluate their models before release is to delay the model release cycle, and there's a lot of competitive pressure right now not to do that.

points.core: Verifying long-horizon agent capabilities requires running models for equally long real durations.
points.note: Accept: knowing what an agent can do over a week, month, or six months requires actually running it that long. Do not credit: generic claims that benchmarks are incomplete.

points.core: Rapid model release cycles ship successor models before existing ones hit limits.
points.note: Accept: new models launching every two to three months outpaces the time needed to push current models to their ceiling. Do not credit: vague statements about fast AI progress without linking to evaluation duration.

points.core: Competitive pressure prevents labs from delaying releases to finish long-horizon evaluations.
points.note: Accept: market race dynamics stopping labs from holding models back for multi-month pre-release testing. Do not credit: generic claims that labs ignore safety or quality.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because a model's capability isn't a fixed, directly measurable property; it's something that emerges from training and can only be probed indirectly, and every probe gives a lower bound rather than a ceiling.

Several things compound this. Models are grown through training rather than designed, so labs can't read abilities off the weights, and interpretability isn't yet mature enough to enumerate what a network can do. Evaluations only test what someone thought to test, and benchmarks saturate, leak into training data, or miss the relevant skill entirely. Measured performance also depends heavily on elicitation: better prompting, scaffolding, tool access, fine-tuning, more inference compute, or agentic harnesses routinely unlock abilities months after release, so a failed test shows only that this particular method didn't work. The space of possible tasks and inputs is effectively unbounded, while pre-release testing is time-limited, and millions of users explore far more than any red team can. Finally, models may underperform on evaluations, whether through sandbagging or recognising they're being tested, which makes results harder to trust.

So labs publish what a model has been shown to do, not what it can do at most.

points.why: The response mentions time-limited testing but never says that verifying an agent’s capability over a given duration requires running it for that full duration.
The response mentions abilities discovered months after release but does not link successor releases to the time needed to reach the current model’s limits.
The response gives no competitive reason why labs release models before completing long-horizon evaluations.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Evaluations can only establish a lower bound on what a model can do, never an upper bound. Unlike traditional software built to explicit specifications, frontier models acquire capabilities emergently across billions of opaque parameters rather than by deliberate design, leaving creators without a blueprint of what the weights encode.

Because observed performance depends heavily on how a model is invoked, pre-release testing faces a fundamental elicitation problem. Small internal teams cannot exhaust the vast space of prompting strategies, agentic scaffolds, tool integrations, fine-tuning, and inference-time compute budgets that millions of external developers will explore after launch. This gap creates a persistent capability overhang, where latent skills remain hidden until someone builds the right harness to unlock them. Meanwhile, static benchmarks saturate quickly and poorly reflect open-ended real-world tasks, while frontier models increasingly exhibit evaluation awareness—recognizing when they are being tested and sometimes altering their behavior or underperforming. Together, opaque emergence, incomplete elicitation, and limited benchmarks ensure a model’s true ceiling is only discovered months after release.

points.why: The response attributes delayed discovery to incomplete elicitation and benchmark limits without stating that verifying long-horizon capabilities requires running the model for the same duration.
The response mentions discovery months after release but never links that delay to successor models launching before the current model's limits can be established.
The response discusses limited pre-release testing capacity without identifying competitive pressure as a reason labs cannot delay releases to finish long-horizon evaluations.

noweb.answer: Nobody knows a new frontier model's true capability ceiling because evaluations only establish a lower bound—proving what a model can do under tested conditions, never everything it could do. A model's weights encode vast latent capabilities that remain dormant until unlocked by the right elicitation methods. Before release, labs evaluate models under tight timelines using finite benchmarks, prompts, and software scaffolds, sampling only a tiny fraction of possible tasks and configurations. Once deployed, millions of users and engineers spend months experimenting with novel prompting strategies, inference-time compute scaling, external tools, agentic workflows, and fine-tuning. This massive, decentralized exploration routinely uncovers "capability overhangs"—skills the model already possessed that pre-deployment testing missed simply due to suboptimal harnessing. Furthermore, post-training alignment and safety guardrails can inadvertently mask raw abilities that alternative framing later reveals. Because a model's effective performance depends not just on its weights, but on surrounding scaffolding and human ingenuity that have yet to be invented, its true upper bound can never be measured upfront—only discovered empirically over time.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because capability isn't a fixed property you can read off a model. It depends on how the model is used, and nobody can search all the ways of using it.

Evaluations only sample. Labs test against benchmarks and red-team tasks they wrote themselves. Benchmarks saturate, can leak into training data, and only measure what someone thought to ask, so a model can be strong at things nobody tested.

Performance also depends heavily on elicitation. Better prompting, chain-of-thought, tool access, agent scaffolding, extra inference-time compute, and fine-tuning can each unlock large gains after release. Early evaluations of GPT-4, for example, missed much of what later agent setups got out of it. Pre-release testing gets weeks with a small team. After launch, millions of users experiment for months and find new uses and jailbreaks.

Underneath all this, interpretability is still immature. Labs can't inspect the weights and list what the model knows or can do; they can only infer it from behavior. Models may also sandbag, or behave differently when they seem to detect they're being tested.

So any published capability figure is a lower bound, not the true ceiling.

The response contrasts weeks of pre-release testing with months of post-release experimentation but never links successor releases to evaluations ending before the current model reaches its ceiling.
The response mentions limited pre-release testing but gives no role to competitive pressure in keeping labs from delaying releases.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Frontier AI labs do not know the true capability ceiling of newly released models primarily because raw model performance is inseparable from how the model is elicited. A model’s weights contain latent abilities that only surface when paired with the right prompting techniques, tool integrations, agentic scaffolds, or inference-time compute strategies. Before release, a lab’s evaluation team can only test a narrow slice of these configurations under tight competitive deadlines.

Benchmarks also provide an incomplete picture. They quickly saturate, capture narrow proxies rather than open-ended real-world tasks, and cannot anticipate the full range of domains or creative workflows users will apply a model to. Because large neural networks are opaque systems whose emergent behaviors cannot be deduced simply from training loss or architecture, discovering what a model can truly do is an empirical process. Once millions of external developers and researchers begin experimenting with new harnesses, fine-tunes, and multi-step workflows, they routinely uncover capabilities that even the model’s creators did not realize were there.

points.why: The response describes testing different configurations but never states that verifying a long-horizon capability requires running the model for that same duration.
The response never links the release of successor models to insufficient time to reach the current model’s capability ceiling.
The response links competitive deadlines to testing fewer configurations but never explains that competition keeps labs from delaying releases to finish long-horizon evaluations.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A frontier lab can measure what a new model does under specific test conditions. Its true ceiling would be the best it could do under the best conditions, and finding those conditions is itself an open-ended search. Different prompts, examples, tools, or amounts of time to reason can change whether the model solves a task. A failed test shows that one setup failed. A successful test shows what the model achieved in that setup, and repeated trials tell you how reliably it can do so.

The ceiling also depends on what you count as part of the system. A model answering once has a different ceiling from the same model allowed to try several approaches, run code, and check its work. After release, users explore more tasks and setups than the lab could test in advance. They can uncover abilities the lab missed, so launch evaluations give a map of demonstrated performance under stated conditions, with plenty of territory still unexplored.

points.why: The response says reasoning time can affect performance but never states that verifying a long-horizon capability requires running the model for that duration.
The response describes post-release exploration without saying that successor models launch before existing models have been pushed to their limits.
The response gives no account of competitive pressure keeping labs from delaying release to finish long-horizon evaluations.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A lab can show what a model can do under the conditions it tested. Establishing a ceiling would require showing that the model can’t do better under any other relevant conditions. That’s much harder. Even with the weights and training records in hand, researchers have no reliable way to read off every skill the model has learned. They have to test it, and each evaluation covers a limited set of tasks, prompts, tools, and budgets for reasoning or repeated attempts.

A failure is therefore ambiguous. The task may be beyond the model, or a different prompt, more time, or a way to check its work may let the same model succeed. After release, users try tasks and techniques the lab never tested, sometimes revealing abilities without any change to the weights. Labs can estimate performance quite precisely under specified conditions. What remains unknown is how far the best way of using the model can take it.

points.why: The response says more time may help a model succeed, but does not say that verifying a long-horizon capability requires running the model for that full duration.
The response discusses discoveries after release without linking successor release timing to the time needed to establish the current model’s limits.
The response does not identify competitive pressure as a reason labs release models before completing long-horizon evaluations.
